result.markdown: --- title: "Federated machine learning with dsFlower" subtitle: "Three algorithms across three hospitals — no patient data ever leaves a site" format: html execute: warning: false message: false error: true --- Download the R script (.R) Source (.Rmd) # Welcome So far in this workshop you have used DataSHIELD to compute **summary statistics** and **regression models** (`ds.glm`) across federated sites. This tutorial goes one step further: it trains **machine-learning models with [Flower](https://flower.ai)** — the popular federated-learning framework — *underneath* DataSHIELD, using the **dsFlower** package. We will train **three different algorithms** and see where each shines: 1. **Logistic regression** — a simple linear classifier, 2. a **neural network** (PyTorch), and 3. **gradient boosting** (XGBoost), on **two datasets**: a breast-cancer cohort (is a tumour malignant?) and handwritten digits (which digit, 0–9?). For each one we will **look at the data first**, **train the model and watch the process**, and then **make predictions** on new, unseen samples. ::: {.callout-important} ## What makes this special No record ever leaves its hospital. Each site trains on its own patients and shares only model updates, and those updates are combined with **Secure Aggregation** — cryptographically masked, so not even the researcher running the training can inspect any single hospital's contribution. Every model below is trained on the pooled population that no one was ever able to pool. ::: # 1. Connect Log in to the three hospitals and load the three tables we will use. Then open the federated channel (a local Flower **SuperLink** that the hospitals connect to). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DSI); library(DSOpal); library(dsBaseClient); library(dsFlowerClient) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} builder <- DSI::newDSLoginBuilder() for (h in c("nairobi", "dakar", "douala")) { builder$append(server = h, url = paste0("https://", h, ".datashield.live"), user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd") } conns <- DSI::datashield.login(logins = builder$build()) DSI::datashield.assign.table(conns, "D", "dsflower_demo.breast_cancer") # tumours (binary) DSI::datashield.assign.table(conns, "G", "dsflower_demo.digits") # digits 0-9 DSI::datashield.assign.table(conns, "G4", "dsflower_demo.digits4") # digits 0-3 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.flower.link.up(conns) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} The SuperLink runs locally on your machine; it is shut down again in the last section. ::: # 2. Logistic regression — predicting malignancy ## Look at the data The **breast-cancer** cohort: 569 tumours described by 30 cell-nucleus measurements, split across the three sites. The target `malignant` is `1` for malignant, `0` for benign. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("D", datasources = conns) # rows per site + pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $`dimensions of D in nairobi` #> [1] 190 31 #> #> $`dimensions of D in dakar` #> [1] 190 31 #> #> $`dimensions of D in douala` #> [1] 189 31 #> #> $`dimensions of D in combined studies` #> [1] 569 31 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.table("D$malignant", datasources = conns) # class balance ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $output.list #> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_row.props #> study #> D$malignant nairobi dakar douala #> 0 0.3333333 0.3333333 0.3333333 #> 1 0.3349057 0.3349057 0.3301887 #> NA NaN NaN NaN #> #> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_col.props #> study #> D$malignant nairobi dakar douala #> 0 0.6263158 0.6263158 0.6296296 #> 1 0.3736842 0.3736842 0.3703704 #> NA 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000 #> #> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts #> study #> D$malignant nairobi dakar douala #> 0 119 119 119 #> 1 71 71 70 #> NA 0 0 0 #> #> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_proportions #> D$malignant #> 0 1 NA #> 0.627 0.373 0.000 #> #> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts #> D$malignant #> 0 1 NA #> 357 212 0 #> #> #> $validity.message #> [1] "Data in all studies were valid" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bc_features <- setdiff(ds.colnames("D", datasources = conns)[[1]], "malignant") length(bc_features) # 30 predictors ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 30 ``` ::: ::: This is a **binary** problem with well-separated classes — exactly what a **logistic regression** does well. ## Train (watch the process) Five rounds of federated averaging with Secure Aggregation. The log shows each round masking and combining the three sites' updates: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bc_fit <- ds.flower.fit( conns, symbol = "D", target = "malignant", features = bc_features, model = "sklearn_logreg", strategy = "fedavg", privacy = "clinical_default", rounds = 5L, verbose = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> nairobi: SuperNode connected ``` ::: ::: ## A note on XGBoost here Under Secure Aggregation each tree is a shallow *stump* trained from a securely-aggregated gradient histogram, and **every class needs its own trees** — powerful, but heavy over the secure channel, which is why we restricted it to four classes. Even so it classifies the held-out samples well. With more rounds (and a faster channel than the one we use to *reach* across NAT) it scales to all ten classes like any boosted model. ::: # 6.
